correctness.rationale: For any binary word the least alternating 01-host length is exactly 1 plus its number of adjacent pairs unequal to 01. For a concatenated q-th power this becomes 1+q*d+(q-1)*e. Tracing powers of the two-by-two weighted edge matrix counts all distinct roots once by first-appearance size and root length. The inverse matrix gives the claimed bivariate rational series; specialization and even-index Fibonacci/Lucas identities yield all q,k values, including empty-host and residue boundaries. Independent direct word enumeration (133 q,k pairs), threshold checks (2,046 binary test words), bivariate length checks and linear-recurrence checks passed; finite checks are not infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Inoue et al. (2018), the closest fully inspected source with the same square-subsequence objects, solves a longest-square optimization problem, not counting all distinct square roots in alternating hosts. Lai et al. (2022) uses letterwise duplications, not repeated arbitrary roots. The older Kosowski (2004) abstract addresses maximum length but its full text was not accessible, so hidden specialization remains a risk. Targeted semantic and literature searches across alternate names, Fibonacci/Lucas sequences, and counting powers revealed no covering count or equivalent root-length rational function. This is a best-knowledge assessment, not proof of global priority.

value.rationale: The exact enumeration fills a nontrivial gap between longest repeated-subsequence optimization and counting all admissible repetitions. The law is an infinite-family, all-exponent classification: first appearance has only two residues modulo q, with Lucas and Fibonacci jump sizes independent of q after rescaling. The complete root-length bivariate spectrum strengthens it beyond a single univariate statistic and supports length-constrained enumeration. This is a motivated counting invariant for tandem subsequences of an elementary periodic host, not arbitrary parameter slicing or a known table recomputation.
